questions.prompt: A JSON Extractor is a child of the 'Login' sampler. Which samples does it process?
options: Every sampler in the Thread Group
Every sampler in the Test Plan
questions.explanation: A post-processor attached to a sampler applies only to that sampler. Placed at Thread Group level it would run after every sampler.

questions.prompt: Where must a Constant Timer go if it should delay only the 'Checkout' request?
options: As a child of the Checkout sampler
questions.explanation: A timer as a sampler's child affects only that sampler. Higher placements put more samplers in its scope.

questions.prompt: Elements inside a Simple Controller apply to the samplers inside that controller only.
questions.explanation: Controllers create a scope: config elements, timers, assertions and processors inside apply to samplers in that branch.

questions.prompt: A JSON Extractor that extracts `id` sits directly under the Thread Group, which has 4 samplers. Only the 2nd response contains `id`. With Default Value `NOT_FOUND`, what is `${id}` after the 4th sampler?
options: NOT_FOUND, because the extractor ran after every sampler and the later responses had no id
The extractor only runs once, so the id is kept
questions.explanation: Group-level post-processors run after each sampler in scope; responses 3 and 4 overwrite the variable with the default. Attach the extractor to the sampler that returns the id.

questions.prompt: Two Response Assertions are in scope of one sampler: one under the Thread Group and one under the sampler. Which run?
options: Only the one under the sampler
Neither until a listener requests it
questions.explanation: All assertions in scope are applied. A sample fails if any assertion fails. Scope is additive, not override-based.

questions.prompt: Which statements about pre-processors are correct? Select all that apply.
options: They run before each sampler in their scope
Several pre-processors in scope run in tree order (outer before inner)
They run before timers in the execution order
They run only once per thread
questions.explanation: Pre-processors fire before every sampler in scope, in the order they appear from outer to inner scope, and before timers. Once-per-thread behaviour is what a Once Only Controller or setUp gives, not pre-processors.

questions.prompt: How long is the total timer delay before 'Pay' runs in each iteration?
questions.code:
Thread Group
  Constant Timer 500 ms
  Simple Controller: Browse
    Constant Timer 200 ms
    HTTP Request: List
  Simple Controller: Buy
    Constant Timer 1000 ms
    HTTP Request: Pay
      Constant Timer 300 ms
questions.explanation: Timers in scope sum up: the group-level 500 ms timer and the controller-level 1,000 ms timer apply to Pay, plus Pay's own 300 ms = 1,800 ms. The Browse timer is outside Pay's scope.

questions.prompt: A Header Manager containing `Authorization: Bearer ${token}` sits under the 'Login' sampler. Every later API call returns 401. What is the fix?
options: Move the Header Manager to the Thread Group (or a controller wrapping the API calls) so it applies to the later samplers
Add a Constant Timer before the API calls
questions.explanation: Config elements under a sampler apply only to that sampler, so the API calls never get the header. Timers, redirects and renaming do not change scope.

coding.title: Which elements apply to a sampler?
coding.prompt:
Model a plan as nested dicts: `{'name': str, 'kind': str, 'children': [...]}`. Kinds are `group`, `controller`, `sampler`, or an element kind such as `timer`, `assertion`, `config`. An element applies to a sampler if it is a **child of the sampler** or a **child of any ancestor** (group/controller) of the sampler.

Write `applies_to(tree, sampler_name)` returning the names of applying non-structural elements (kinds other than group/controller/sampler), ordered outermost first, then tree order.

Example: for a group with timer `T1`, a controller holding timer `T2` and sampler `Pay` (which has timer `T3`), `applies_to(tree, 'Pay')` is `['T1', 'T2', 'T3']`.
coding.explanation: Walking down the tree while carrying the elements collected from each ancestor reproduces JMeter's scoping rule: an element affects everything below its parent.
hints: Write a recursive function that carries a list of inherited element names.
At each node, add its non-structural children to the inherited list before descending.
When you reach the target sampler, return inherited plus its own children.

tests.name: Nested timers
tests.code:
tree = {'name':'TG','kind':'group','children':[
 {'name':'T1','kind':'timer'},
 {'name':'Browse','kind':'controller','children':[{'name':'TB','kind':'timer'},{'name':'List','kind':'sampler','children':[]}]},
 {'name':'Buy','kind':'controller','children':[{'name':'T2','kind':'timer'},{'name':'Pay','kind':'sampler','children':[{'name':'T3','kind':'timer'}]}]}]}
assert applies_to(tree, 'Pay') == ['T1','T2','T3'], applies_to(tree, 'Pay')
assert applies_to(tree, 'List') == ['T1','TB']

tests.name: Siblings excluded
tests.code:
tree = {'name':'TG','kind':'group','children':[
 {'name':'A','kind':'sampler','children':[{'name':'Hdr','kind':'config'}]},
 {'name':'B','kind':'sampler','children':[]},
 {'name':'Check','kind':'assertion'}]}
assert applies_to(tree, 'B') == ['Check'], applies_to(tree, 'B')
assert applies_to(tree, 'A') == ['Check','Hdr']

coding.title: Total timer delay per iteration
coding.prompt:
Every timer in scope of a sampler runs before it, and their delays add up. Write `iteration_delay(samplers)` where `samplers` is a list of lists: each inner list holds the delays (ms) of the timers in scope of one sampler. Return the total delay one iteration spends in timers.

Example: `[[500], [500, 1000, 300]]` returns `2300`.
coding.solution:
def iteration_delay(samplers):
    return sum(sum(timers) for timers in samplers)
coding.explanation: A group-level timer is in scope of every sampler, so it is paid once per sampler, not once per iteration. Summing per sampler makes that visible: one 500 ms group timer over 10 samplers costs 5 s per iteration.
hints: Sum the timers for each sampler.
